item.title: MAN. I think dead internet theory is correct, I think the adage "if it feels too good to be true" needs to be followed closely, and that nothing online is trustworthy now means after 40 years of being online, it's going to make me stop using the internet.
item.description:
FAKE. I fell in love with this cute pup on an instagram my wife sent. I fully believed it for about a minute... then looked at the account selling the life vest, which had dozens and dozens of IDENTICAL videos with different dog breeds. 85 posts in one month. Impossible. The company is new, the website is sketchy, it's all social media AI Slop ad scams on instagram. it's CRAZY. But I really couldn't tell for a bit, and I'm not lazy or bad at this. But I don't want to use the internet where you have to doubt everything for minutes at a time.
If people create something with no effort, it has no value. Why would I want to be subjected to this slop without my consent? What in the hell are platforms thinking? What are these technologists thinking... because they're ruining the internet. And one giddy bad actor can launch score of these fake website companies, exponentially destroying the usability of the internet. When the utility of the internet is broken, and you need to spend 10 minutes figuring out if a harmless, meaningless video is real... It is as over as shell art. Cooked, as they say. It's pretty surreal how quickly the internet degraded. First enshittification, then organic search... but holy crap it's unusable. Why is Silicon Valley constantly answering questions no one asked? Weirdos.

item.description: I can still remember how different that gold cartridge felt from every other Nintendo game I owned. Before I even pressed Start, The Legend of Zelda already felt like something important. As a kid, I would sit on the floor way too close to the TV and disappear into Hyrule for hours. Most of the time I had absolutely no idea where I was going. I burned random bushes, bombed every wall that looked suspicious and wandered around as Link hoping I would accidentally discover a hidden cave, a new item or another piece of the Triforce. There were no easy answers. You learned secrets from a friend at school, scribbled notes on paper and raced home to see if the rumor was actually true. Every discovery felt like it belonged to you. The Legend of Zelda was released in the US 39 years ago today, and I can still hear that opening music in my head. That original NES game did not just feel like something I played. It felt like my own adventure. Who else remembers seeing that gold cartridge for the first time?
